As with any electronic equipment, an analysis of the circuitry is necessary for full understanding of how the system operates.
INTRODUCTIONM
For a technician, this is important. It's nearly impossible to effectively troubleshoot any equipment if you don't know how it works.

SSB communication systems are no different than any other piece of equipment when troubleshooting. Many of the components and circuit functions of SSB systems are identical to AM Broadcast formats but there are major differences that must be explored and understood.
Let's begin the lesson on SSB ANALYSIS....................................
LESSON MENU
SSB SCHEMATIC ANALYSIS
Transmitter Operations: The first thing you may have noticed about the NIDA SSB Communication System is that it contains 6 individual PC130 cards.
DISCUSSION

Unlike AM and FM broadcast signals, and even CB, SSB signals are not an abundant RF component of our airspace. Because of this, you have been given cards that generate SSB signals, either with voice or signal generator.
You may also have noticed that there is no channel selector or other tuning device. Located on the PC130-450 card are a microphone and several switches.

The condenser microphone is your input device for voice generated audio and the switches provide a choice for external generator or internal 400 or 1 kHz audio tones from an on-board signal generator.
Looking first at the schematic for the PC130-450 card, we'll begin with X1, the condenser microphone.
Sound enters the microphone and is converted to AF. The signal then enters the audio amplifier, U1, at Pin 3. The sensitivity of the amplifier is adjustable at the variable resistor, R10.

Having been amplified, the signal leaves U1 at Pin 6 and is sent to S2. This switch allows you to select between the signal generator and the microphone. With the switch in the microphone position, the signal then is routed to S3.
S3 is marked as Ext./Int. When the switch is in the internal position the signal produced by either the microphone or the
on-board signal generator is allowed to pass on to Pin T.

Pin T is the output of the card and feeds to Pin E, PC130-451 card. When S3 is in the "EXT" position, an external generator can be used, providing a source of greater flexibility than the options from the on-board generator.

Before moving on to the PC130-451 card, a quick overview of the signal generator circuitry is desirable. U2 is the heart of the generator and, by itself, is nothing more than a differential amplifier.

U2, Pin 7, is the input for the positive voltage and is configured in a feedback loop from the output. When switch S1 is in the up (400 Hz) position, resistors R5 and R7 are selected. These resistors, in conjunction with C7 and C10, develop a 400 Hz signal.
When S1 is in the down (1 kHz) position, resistors R6 and R8 are connected to the circuit and with C10 and C7, produce a 1 kHz signal.
Were it not for D1, D2, and R9, both the 400 Hz and 1 kHz signals would be square waves. However, with the presence of those components, the square wave is converted to a sine wave.
When the signal leaves the PC130-450 card, it enters the
PC130-451card at Pin E. At this point in the generation process, the signal isn't quite strong enough and must be amplified.

This job is performed by U1. The audio enters U1 at Pin 3. U1 can be trimmed by adjusting the variable resistor R1. After amplification, the audio (modulating signal) is now ready to be mixed with the control signal.

The control signal (sometimes referred to as a sub-carrier) is accomplished by Y1 and U2. Y1 is a 1.8432 MHz crystal oscillator tied to the on-board oscillator amp within U2, a 14 bit binary ripple counter.
The frequency output of the counter at U2, Pin 6 has been divided down to 14.4 kHz and can be measured at TP3.
In order for the mixer operation to take place, four different phases must be developed. This task is performed by the two
Through the use of feedback and the Q's and Q's, four separate phases are created, each a 90
shift apart. That is, 0, 90, 180, and 270 degrees..
These signals can be measured and viewed on an oscilloscope at test points 4, 5, 6, and 7.
The 90 degree shifted signals should appear similar to the waveforms shown in the timing diagram below.

From the two D F/F's, the signal (having been split into four separate phases) enters two mixers. While there is mixing action taking place, the primary purpose of this circuit is to ensure a 90 degree phase shift in the signal between TP9 and TP8.
Each mixer is made up of four analog switches and a transformer. This first mixer consists of U4a through U4d and T1, the second, U5a through U5d and T2.

Each switch uses a control line to allow the switch to pass the signal. When the control line is high, the switch closes and the signal passes. Conversely, when the control line is low, the switch opens and there is not output.
When the switch is closed, the control signal is also passed; mixing with the audio signal. The result of the digital control signal and the analog input is shown below.
Upon leaving the PC130-451 card, the two signals (shifted by 90 degrees) enter the PC130-452 card at Pins E and D. All circuitry between Pin E and TP1 make up an active low-pass filter.
Identical circuitry can be seen between Pin D and TP4. The purpose of the filters is to smooth out the signal coming from the previous stage.
The filtering effect can easily be viewed by placing one scope probe on Pin E of PC130-452 and a second probe on TP1.

The 90 degree phase shift remains, but the decidedly digital appearance of the signal, before the filter, is converted to a more analogous waveform once passing through it. After being "smoothed", the signals are prepared for mixing with the carrier.
IC2 is the 40 MHz carrier oscillator. From its output at Pin 4, the signal is used as a clock for the D F/F divider circuit.
This circuit is used in the same way that the divider on
PC130-451 is used to develop four phases of the same signal,
90 degrees apart. In the process, however, the frequency is divided down to 10 MHz.
The separate phases can be measured at TP2, TP3, U6a Pin 5 and U6b Pin 8. The 180 and 270 degree shifted signals are not used, only the 0 and 90 degree signals are fed to the mixers.
Unlike the analog switches used earlier on PC130-451, U3 and U4 are conventional mixers identical to the mixers used by the AM, FM and CB radios already covered in the Communications module.

The 10 MHz carrier signal is fed into the Oscillator 1 (OSC1) input of both mixers (Pin 6). The only difference between the two is the 90 degree shift. This means that the dual audio and carrier signals are 90 degrees out of phase.
The audio enters the mixers at Pin 1 (the INA inputs) and mixes with the carrier. The resultant signal can be seen at Pins 4 and 5 of both mixers, TP's 5, 6, and 7.

Notice switch S1 on the output of U4. This switch allows the user to select which sideband to transmit. By placing the switch in the up position you select the USB and in the down position, the lower sideband.
The signal path from U4 is dependent on the switch position of S1. Regardless of which sideband is selected, the signal must pass through a variable resistor.
R9 is for the LSB adjustment, while R10 adjusts the signal for the USB. Whichever sideband is selected, the opposite will be cancelled out in the summing amplifier, U5.
After leaving the summing amplifier at Pin 7, the signal passes through a tunable bandpass filter consisting of L1 and C20; C19 is a coupling capacitor. This filter is adjusted for 10 MHz.

Receiver Operations: The dissection of a single sideband receiver reveals an almost mirror image of the transmitter. The components are nearly identical, just in a reverse order.
One of the unique aspects of the SSB Receiver is that the carrier signal must be recreated in the receiver in order for the intelligence to be detected.
Unlike AM broadcast signals where the carrier is transmitted in tact, SSB has no carrier in that sense. The carrier is only present when a modulating signal is present.
As a consequence, the SSB receiver will have no reference unless the carrier is reinserted into the signal upon its arrival in the receiver.

The transmitted SSB signal enters the receiver at TP1 of the PC130-453 card and is immediately met by another tunable filter made up of L1 and C2 identical to the filter it passed through just prior to transmission.
After the filter, the signal splits to a parallel path and enters two mixer/amplifiers, U1 and U2 at Pin 1.
IC1, U5a and U5b make up the RF generator (oscillator) that inserts the carrier back into the intelligence. IC1 (the actual oscillator) outputs a 40 MHz signal at Pin 4.

This signal is fed to two D F/F's for use as the clock signal. Here, the frequency is divided out to 10 MHz. Like the D F/F network in the transmitter, the output takes the carrier and delivers it in four phases, 90 degrees apart.
In this instance, only the 0 and 90 degrees shifted signals are used. Test points 4 and 5 may be used to view these signals. Upon leaving the F/F's, the 0
phase signal is fed to Pin 6 (OSC 1) on the mixer U1, and the 90
phase is fed to Pin 6 (OSC 1) on mixer U2.
The outputs of the mixers are the demodulated intelligence
90 degrees out of phase. The first mixer, (U1) passes the signal from the output at Pin 5 directly to Pin 2, U3, an active low-pass filter/amplifier.

The second mixer (U2) outputs on Pins 4 and 5 which are connected to S1. The switch accommodates the selection of either the USB or LSB. Obviously, if the LSB was, in fact, the transmitted signal, this switch must be adjusted to select the lower sideband.
2. The low-pass filter/amplifiers boost the signa)

After leaving the switch S1, the signal goes to an active low-pass filter/amplifier U4, Pin 2. The signal from U1, Pin 5 goes to another low-pass filter/amplifier U3, Pin 2. The low-pass filter/amplifiers boost the signals to approximately 0.85 VAC.

The two 90 degree phase shifted signals leave PC130-453 at Pins T and U and enter the PC130-454 card at Pins E and D. Upon arrival at Pins E and D, the signals are routed through low-pass filters consisting of R1, C1 and R3, C2.

From here, the signals pass into two active low-pass filters/amplifiers, U1 and U2. These filters are set to pass the 1MHz signals and, at the same time, increase the gain. C20 and C21 are coupling capacitors for the mixers.
A sub-carrier is needed to re-create the four phases 90 degrees apart, just as it was during the transmission process. Y1, U7 and U6a and U6b perform this task.

The signal Y1, a 1.8432 MHz crystal enters U7, Pin11, a divide by N counter. Only output Q7 at U7, Pin6 is used to provide a clock signal for D F/F's U6A and U6B.put at Pin 6 is used as a clock signal for a pair of D F/F's.

Feedback from Q , output of U6b Pin 8, ensures the14.4 kHz signal is divided into four 3.6 kHz signals of 0, 90, 180, and 270 degree phase, measured at test points 4, 5, 6, and 7.nd 7...

While the frequency at the four test points is the same, the phase of the signal at the test points has been shifted by 90 degrees. The 90 degree shift in the signals may be seen by using the dual trace function of the oscilloscope.
Where a four channel oscilloscope is available, all four test points may be viewed simultaneously. Each phase of the signal feeds to a different pair of analog switches which make up the two mixers.
At this point the four 3.6 kHz 90 degree shifted audio signals and sub-carrier are filtered and enter two mixer's U3 and U4.and U4b.

The phased sub-carrier enters the mixers as a control signal and mixes with the audio, ultimately producing two completely reconstructed SSB signals 90 degrees apart. These signals can be seen at TP8 and 9.

Following the transformers, a summing amplifier (U5), combines the two signals, favoring the selected sideband of the transmitter and receiver (USB or LSB). The signal leaves U5, Pin 6 at PC 130-454 at Pin T and enters PC 130-455 at Pin E.
The PC130-455 card contains a low-pass filter and an audio power amplifier. The low-pass filter is tunable by adjusting R3, a 10 kW variable resistor. Volume at the speaker is adjusted by R4.
This completes the information on SSB SCHEMATIC ANALYSIS...

The signals you observed and measured in the transmitter are recreated in the receiver and so not as much time will be spent in that pursuit. However, you will be able to observe the signal reconstruction.

Following TP1 on PC130-453, the receiver's antenna input, is a tunable circuit consisting of C1 and L1. As with the tunable circuit at the transmitter's antenna, this should be tuned for maximum signal.
